chief_complaint: spreading red, hot, swollen skin plaque on shin
hpi_details: 50-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled diabetes presents with a 2-day history of an expanding, unilateral, red, hot, swollen, and painful plaque on his right lower leg. He has a history of tinea pedis (athlete's foot) between his toes. Accompanied by fever and chills.
ideas: He thinks a poisonous spider bit his shin while he was clearing brush in the yard or that his athlete's foot spread up his leg.
concerns: He is worried that he might lose his leg to an amputation like his older brother did from diabetes.
expectations: He hopes to get a strong prescription antibiotic ointment or pills so he will not lose his job as a delivery driver.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Cellulitis (lower extremity) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Cellulitis lower extremity: Oral Cephalexin 500mg QID for 7-10 days, elevate leg, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: spreading red, hot, swollen skin plaque on shin

Key HPI features: A 50-year-old male with poorly controlled diabetes presents with a 2-day history of an expanding, unilateral, red, hot, swollen, and painful plaque on his right lower leg, with a history of tinea pedis between the toes. Accompanied by fever and chills.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.5C, HR 105. Right lower extremity shows a poorly demarcated, warm, erythematous, edematous, tender plaque extending from the ankle to mid-calf. Cracking and maceration in the toe web spaces (portal of entry).
Relevant background/PMH: Poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes mellitus
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Cellulitis (lower extremity).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to DVT without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Pain out of proportion or rapid spread.
management_principles: Initiate empiric oral antibiotics (Cephalexin 500mg QID for 7-10 days) covering streptococci and MSSA; elevate the affected leg.
Treat the underlying tinea pedis with topical antifungal therapy to eliminate the portal of entry and reduce recurrence risk.
Outline the borders of erythema and reassess within 48 hours; escalate to IV therapy or admission if there is rapid spread, systemic toxicity, or poor glycemic control.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 50M diabetic presenting with acute onset of fever and a rapidly spreading, painful, erythematous rash on the right lower leg.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 38.5C, HR 105. Right lower extremity shows a poorly demarcated, warm, erythematous, edematous, tender plaque extending from the ankle to the mid-calf. Cracking and maceration noted in the web spaces between toes.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Bacterial Cellulitis of the lower extremity.
reference_soap.plan: Initiate empiric oral antibiotics covering streptococci and MSSA (e.g., Cephalexin). Treat the underlying tinea pedis with topical Terbinafine to eliminate the portal of entry. Elevate the leg. Outline the borders with a marker to monitor for spread.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Cellulitis lower extremity
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Cellulitis lower extremity
Implement evidence-based management plan: Oral Cephalexin 500mg QID for 7-10 days, elevate leg

teaching.one_liner: Streptococcal or staphylococcal bacteria enter through a skin break, causing a spreading red, hot, swollen plaque.
red_flags: Pain out of proportion or rapid spread

must_ask.say: Was there any cut or injury to the skin there?
How fast has the redness been spreading?

history.answer: My right lower leg has become bright red, swollen, and hot to the touch over the past two days, and it hurts a lot when I stand or walk on it.
It started two days ago as a small red patch near my right ankle and quickly climbed up to the middle of my calf.
It is only on my right shin and lower leg; my left leg looks and feels completely normal.
It is a solid red, swollen plaque that feels hot and tense, but there are no blisters or open scabs on the surface.
It is a throbbing, aching pain that feels like burning heat, around a six out of ten, and it throbs worse whenever my foot is down.
It expanded quite rapidly, spreading several inches upward within just forty-eight hours.
No, it has stayed constantly swollen and red; it does not come and go or vanish in hours like hives.
I have had itchy, peeling, and cracked skin between my toes from athlete's foot for months, but I haven't had any cuts or scrapes on my leg.
history.topic: Portal of entry and skin breaks

history.answer: I have never experienced a red, swollen leg like this before in my life.
Yes, I started having shaking chills and a high fever yesterday afternoon, along with feeling very weak and exhausted.
No, I don't have any blisters, sores, or ulcers in my mouth, eyes, or genital area.
No, the skin is tight and red, but it is not peeling off, blistering, or showing dark purple or black spots.
No, my lips and tongue are not swollen, my throat feels fine, and I have no trouble breathing or wheezing.
I haven't started any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, gout pills, or pain relievers recently.
No, I haven't used any new soaps, detergents, cosmetics, or lotions, and I haven't worn new metal jewelry or touched plants.
Nobody in my household or at my office has any rash, skin infection, or fever.
No, I haven't had any tick or bug bites, and I haven't been hiking in tall grass, swimming, or traveling.
No, I have never had eczema, asthma, or allergic rhinitis.
My knee and ankle joints move fine and don't hurt inside, and my toenails haven't changed except for the peeling skin between my toes.
I put a little bit of over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream on my shin yesterday thinking it was an itch, but it didn't help at all.
I am married and only sexually active with my wife, and I have never had genital ulcers, sores, or discharges.
I have had type 2 diabetes for about seven years, but I must admit my blood sugar control has not been very good lately.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I take metformin 500 milligrams twice a day for my blood sugar, and no other regular prescriptions or supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked in my life.
I only drink an occasional beer with friends once or twice a month, nothing heavy.
I work as an office administrator sitting at a desk, and I live with my wife in an apartment.
My father had type 2 diabetes, but no one in my family has had severe skin problems or autoimmune diseases.

I thought maybe a venomous spider bit my leg while I was cleaning out the garden, or that my athlete's foot fungus somehow crawled up my shin. I'm really worried that this might lead to having my leg amputated, just like what happened to my older brother with diabetes.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 38.5°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Patient appears acutely uncomfortable, flushed, and mildly diaphoretic, favoring his right leg.
Right lower extremity shows a poorly demarcated, warm, erythematous, edematous plaque extending from the ankle to the mid-calf, with cracking and maceration noted in the web spaces between the toes.
Marked tenderness, induration, and warmth over the right anterior and medial lower leg without palpable crepitus, bullae, or fluctuance.
Moderate unilateral soft tissue swelling of the right lower leg; left lower leg has no edema.
Tender, mildly enlarged lymph nodes palpable in the right inguinal region; no hernias noted.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable and symmetric bilaterally.
Conjunctivae are clear without pallor, petechiae, or icterus.
Oral mucosa and lips are pink and moist without ulcerations, swelling, or mucosal lesions.
